Whether heated gemstones are less valuable depends significantly on the specific gemstone type and the nature of the treatment applied. As a general principle, untreated gemstones are considered the most valuable, and the more treatments a stone has undergone, the lower its retail value [d4]; for example, a heated citrine cabochon is less valuable than a natural one of the same quality [d1]. For rubies and sapphires specifically, heating typically causes a loss of roughly half the stone's value compared to an unheated equivalent [d8], and unheated rubies can command dramatically higher prices — a 2-carat unheated Burmese ruby may reach $25,000 per carat versus $7,000 for a heated one [d3]; similarly, an unheated 1-carat ruby with certification may start at $5,000 or more, while a heat-only treated one might sell for $2,000 or more [d6]. However, the impact of heating is not universal: for tanzanite, aquamarine, garnet, tourmaline, and zircon, heating has no impact on value [d8][d5], partly because it is impossible to scientifically distinguish naturally heated from man-heated tanzanite [d5]. It is also important to distinguish between standard heat treatment — which is considered permissible and very common in the trade — and more invasive treatments like beryllium diffusion or glass-filling, which can render a stone essentially worthless as a gem [d6][d9].
